In the general case, it defines a Jacobi structure; to allow for a similar construction to define a Jacobi structure in the general case, Jacobi structures supported in non-trivial line bundles (as mentioned in Remark \ref{rmk-Jacobi}) are needed.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: The definition of Jacobi structure presented here is not the general one, which should allow for Jacobi brackets on the module of sections of a line bundle

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims that the displayed pair constructed from a local contact form defines an ordinary Jacobi structure in the general contact case. Under the old paper's definition, an ordinary Jacobi structure is a global pair of fields, while the preceding sentence only supports that pair when the contact form is global and Remark rmk-Jacobi says that the general case requires a line-bundle-valued Jacobi structure. Thus the claimed general global scope exceeds what the old definitions support.
issues.overall_effect: The example incorrectly extends the ordinary global pair construction to contact structures lacking a global contact form. No later formal result depends on that extra clause because the paper works in local trivializations.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Delete the clause “In the general case, it defines a Jacobi structure.” Retain that a global contact form defines an ordinary Jacobi pair, while the general contact case requires the line-bundle-valued notion described in Remark rmk-Jacobi.
issues.why_classification: The clause directly contradicts both the remainder of its own sentence and the preceding definition and remark. The old source uniquely forces this editorial deletion, and no mathematical inference or dependent result requires repair.

issues.title: Karasev source and target signs are reversed

diagnostic_evidence.quote: since $\omega_{can} = dx\wedge d\xi_x + dt\wedge d\xi_t$ is $1$-homogeneous

issues.failure_explanation: With ω_can=dy^a∧dξ_a, the induced canonical bracket has {y^i,ξ_j}_can=−δ^i_j. For the old α^i=y^i+(1/2)π^{vi}ξ_v+O(ξ²), evaluating at the zero section gives {α^i,α^j}_can=−π^{ij}, so α has the anti-Poisson orientation despite being declared Poisson. Replacing the correction by −(1/2)π^{vi}ξ_v gives +π^{ij}; the corresponding explicit α and β signs must be adjusted so that β(x,ξ)=α(x,−ξ).
issues.overall_effect: The displayed approximation assigns the source map the target orientation, and the old contact-coordinate maps are not a consistent Poisson/anti-Poisson pair. The general existence theorem for homogeneous bi-realizations is independent of this explicit sign error.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Use the convention-consistent Karasev source expansion beginning α^i(y,ξ)=y^i−(1/2)π^{vi}ξ_v, and make the corresponding sign corrections throughout the explicit contact-coordinate source and target formulas while retaining β(y,ξ)=α(y,−ξ).
issues.why_classification: A first-order canonical-bracket calculation is needed to detect and coordinate the source-target correction, so this is more than a purely transcriptional error. The repair is nevertheless short and local, preserves the intended bi-realization and homogeneity guarantees, and does not affect the general existence theorem or any listed dependent result.

issues.title: Lagrangian bisections need a homogeneity hypothesis

failure_location.quote: given a bisection $L$, the inverse restricted to $L$, $\alpha^{-1}_{|L}$ is also homogeneous

diagnostic_evidence.quote: This embedding is homogeneous if and only if $\varphi$ is homogeneous:

issues.failure_explanation: From equivariance of α, applying the lifted action to α⁻¹ restricted to L produces a point in the transformed bisection T*h_z(L), not necessarily in L. Hence the asserted inverse is equivariant only when L is invariant. A concrete counterexample is the pair groupoid of the homogeneous symplectic manifold with coordinates (x,t), t nonzero, form dt∧dx, and action h_z(x,t)=(x,zt): the symplectomorphism φ(x,t)=(x+log|t|,t) has a Lagrangian graph bisection but does not commute with h, so its induced map is not homogeneous.
issues.overall_effect: Item (1) overstates the result for arbitrary Lagrangian bisections. The ordinary Poisson conclusion remains valid, but homogeneity requires a homogeneous bisection. Subsequent constructions already use homogeneous Lagrangian bisections.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Revise the preceding remark and proposition to state that an arbitrary Lagrangian bisection induces a Poisson diffeomorphism and retains the stated leaf conclusion, while homogeneity of the induced map is asserted only when the bisection is itself invariant under the lifted action.
issues.why_classification: Equivariance of the restricted inverse genuinely requires invariance of the bisection. Nonhomogeneous Lagrangian bisections form a natural, substantial class, so adding homogeneity is a real but limited restriction rather than a technical exceptional-case qualification. The corrected proposition remains recognizably comparable and all subsequent uses already satisfy the added condition, so no global reconstruction is needed.

issues.title: Homogeneous Poincaré proof omits the exactness argument

failure_location.quote: We want to prove that $\pi_*(h_z^*(\alpha)) = h_z^*(\pi_*(\alpha)).$

diagnostic_evidence.quote: The fiber operator $\pi_*$ is defined by

issues.failure_explanation: The lemma claims both exactness and a homogeneous primitive. Its proof starts with an arbitrary form on U×[0,1], defines π_*, and establishes only π_*h_z^*=h_z^*π_*. It never defines a contraction map from U×[0,1] to U, relates the lemma's closed form to the form being integrated, invokes the fiber-homotopy identity, or produces a primitive. Thus the displayed equivariance calculation does not imply the claimed exactness.
issues.overall_effect: The lemma's conclusion is true, but its v1 proof does not establish either the existence of a primitive or its relation to the input form. Later arguments use at most the correctly shown equivariance calculation rather than the missing exactness step.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the incomplete fiber-integration argument by the standard generator argument: for a closed 1-homogeneous form ω and the infinitesimal generator Z of the action, homogeneity gives L_Zω=ω, while Cartan’s formula gives ω=d(i_Zω). Since Z is invariant, i_Zω is also 1-homogeneous.
issues.why_classification: The old proof genuinely omits the step establishing exactness, so the defect is not a typo. A complete proof is supplied by a short, routine Cartan-formula argument requiring no new lemma or construction and preserving the lemma exactly, with no affected downstream chain.

issues.title: The tubular-neighborhood theorem overclaims a uniform radius

failure_location.quote: Then, for $\epsilon$ sufficiently small, each $p\in \mathcal{U}^\epsilon$ has a unique nearest point $q\in X$.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: let $\epsilon:X\rightarrow \mathbb{R}^+$ be a $0$-homogeneous continuous function which tends to zero fast enough as $x$ tends to infinity.

issues.failure_explanation: The statement claims one constant ε works globally, but the proof supports only a function ε(x). For an admissible counterexample, take M=ℝ²×ℝ^× with action on the last factor and invariant metric dx²+dy²+(dt/t)², and let X be the product with ℝ^× of the two curves y=±e^{-x}. Points (x,0,1) have two symmetric nearest points on X at distance at most e^{-x}. Hence every positive constant-radius neighborhood contains points with nonunique nearest points. A radius that shrinks with the base point avoids this obstruction.
issues.overall_effect: The constant-radius nearest-point conclusion fails on general noncompact homogeneous submanifolds. The later normal-form arguments only require a variable-radius homogeneous tubular neighborhood and therefore survive the corrected statement.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restate the theorem using a positive 0-homogeneous radius function ε:X→R_{>0}, define the neighborhood by d(p,q)<ε(q), and justify the choice of ε from local tubular radii using an invariant metric and invariant partition of unity. Retain the unique nearest-point projection and equivariant exponential-map conclusions on this variable-radius neighborhood.
issues.why_classification: Replacing a uniform constant radius by a variable radius removes a genuine global guarantee on the natural class of noncompact homogeneous submanifolds, so the change is not a typo or lossless local repair. The weakening is limited and leaves a recognizably comparable homogeneous tubular-neighborhood theorem sufficient for all later arguments, with only a contained standard construction rather than global proof reconstruction.
